*   **Memory Complexity:** Fixed memory per pixel: $k$ entries [S4].

The evidence explicitly states that the k-buffer stores a 'fixed number of fragments' (specifically k) per pixel. Section 3.2 notes: 'The k-buffer is a fragment stream sorter that works as follows. The claim accurately reflects that the memory complexity is fixed per pixel with k entries.

It is chosen when the fragment stream is approximately sorted (k-nearly sorted), allowing exact visibility sorting on the GPU with $O(n)$ complexity, whereas the unbounded A-buffer requires potentially unbounded memory and the Z-buffer only handles single-layer visibility [S2, unofficial][S4][S5, unofficial].

The claim is fully supported by the provided evidence. Source [S2] and [S4] explicitly state that the k-buffer allows for exact visibility sorting on the GPU with O(n) complexity when the fragment stream is k-nearly sorted. Both sources also contrast this with the original A-buffer, noting that the A-buffer requires potentially unbounded memory, while the k-buffer uses a fixed amount. Source [S5] supports the part of the claim regarding the Z-buffer by describing it as a generalized Z-buffer where the classic Z-buffer corresponds to k=1, implying it handles single-layer visibility.

It acts as a hardware-efficient alternative to the unbounded A-buffer by storing only a constant number $k$ of fragments per pixel, combining incoming fragments with stored ones and discarding the farthest (for front-to-back) or closest (for back-to-front) to manage memory [S2, unofficial][S4].

The claim states that the k-buffer acts as a hardware-efficient alternative to the unbounded A-buffer by storing a constant number k of fragments per pixel, combining incoming fragments with stored ones, and discarding the farthest (for front-to-back) or closest (for back-to-front) to manage memory. Source [S2] explicitly states: 'The k-buffer approach stores only a fixed number of fragments and works by combining the current fragments and discarding some of them as new fragments arrive. This technique reduces the memory requirement...' and 'For front-to-back compositing, each time a new fragment fnew is inserted in the k-buffer, it dislodges the first entry (f1).' Source [S4] notes also confirm: 'A fragment stream sorter that stores a fixed number k of fragments per pixel. It combines incoming fragments with stored ones, discarding the farthest (for front-to-back) or closest (for back-to-front) to manage memory, unlike the unbounded A-buffer.' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

The text explicitly says: 'n1 closest fragment fnew, f1, f2, or f3' followed by '(r1,r2,r3) = remaining fragments'. This confirms that the process of identifying remaining fragments is part of the described algorithm.
